Name: layerwise_language_emergence
Title: Rise, Fade, Return: The Layerwise Life Cycle of Language-Specific Information
Short Hypothesis: Language-specific information follows a non-monotonic layer trajectory: strong in early layers (surface/script), suppressed in middle layers (shared concept computation), and re-emerging in late layers (language-specific generation), producing a characteristic U-shaped decodability curve that marks the shared-computation window.
Related Work: Wendler et al. and logit-lens studies hint at a language-agnostic middle. We rigorously chart the full layerwise decodability of language identity and content, characterizing the U-shape and testing whether the middle 'trough' is the causal shared-computation window, unifying scattered observations into a quantitative life cycle.
Abstract: When is a multilingual model most language-agnostic? We hypothesize language-specific information has a U-shaped layer profile: high early (script/surface), minimal in the middle (shared conceptual computation), and rising again late (target-language generation). Using parallel multilingual text, we decode language identity at each layer with probes and, in parallel, decode language-independent content, expecting an inverse relationship. We predict a decodability trough in the middle layers coinciding with peak shared-concept decodability. Causally, we test whether the middle trough is the shared-computation window: cross-lingual patching and concept editing should succeed maximally at trough layers and fail at high-language-decodability layers. We quantify trough location and depth across model sizes and relate it to cross-lingual transfer quality (deeper/wider trough -> better transfer). Metrics: layerwise language-ID vs content decodability curves, trough layer and depth, cross-lingual patch success by layer, and correlation of trough characteristics with transfer. This provides a unifying quantitative description of where multilingual abstraction happens and a principled target layer for cross-lingual interventions.
Experiments: Extract activations for parallel multilingual text across all layers.
Probe language-ID decodability and content decodability per layer; plot curves.
Identify U-shape: trough layer and depth; test inverse relation with content decodability.
Causal validation: cross-lingual patching and concept editing success by layer; expect peak at trough.
Vary model size; track trough location/depth.
Correlate trough characteristics with cross-lingual transfer performance.
Controls: monolingual model (no trough expected in same sense); shuffled labels.
Risk Factors and Limitations: Probe decodability depends on probe capacity, biasing curve shape.
Content decodability is hard to define independently of language.
Trough may be gradual, making 'shared window' fuzzy.
Scale trends may not be monotonic.
